1177.title: Chesed and Gevurah
1177.hook: Chesed and Gevurah: giving freely, and holding back
1177.carry: chesed gives freely; gevurah gives it shape
1177.tomorrow: Tiferet, the heart of the tree
1177.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often speak of acts of chesed, loving-kindness, such as visiting the sick and feeding guests; in Kabbalah and Hasidic thought, Chesed and Gevurah are taught as a pair of qualities a person learns to balance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown: will above thought, then wisdom's flash and understanding's unfolding. Your line: the flash and the unfolding. Today, below the top three, a pair.

A river with no banks isn't a river. It's a flood. It goes everywhere, soaks everything, and reaches nothing in particular. A river that's all banks and no water is just a ditch. What makes a river is both: the water that wants to pour out, and the edges that give it a direction. Parents know this one. So do good friends, and good teachers. Give with no limit and the gift drowns the person. Hold back with no love and the limit turns cruel.
screen: `NO BANKS: A FLOOD.` → `ALL BANKS: A DITCH.` → `A RIVER NEEDS BOTH.`

segments.voice: Chesed. Love, kindness, giving freely. And its partner, Gevurah: strength, restraint, holding back. First, where they sit. On the kabbalists' map, Chesed is on the right and Gevurah on the left, like two arms. One reaches out. One holds firm. Second, their faces. Chesed is linked to Abraham, whose tent in Genesis is open, who runs to feed three strangers in the heat of the day. The prophet Micah closes his book saying God will perform "the mercy to Abraham", and in Hebrew that mercy is chesed. Gevurah is linked to Isaac, the son who was bound on the altar and lived. Jacob even calls God "the fear of Isaac". Kindness and awe, two fathers, two sides. Third, the images. Kabbalists pair Chesed with water, which flows to whatever is lowest, and Gevurah with fire, which burns away and draws lines. Water alone floods. Fire alone scorches. Fourth, the surprise. Gevurah isn't the villain. Limits are a kind of care. A parent who says not tonight, a friend who says I won't help you do that, a teacher who returns your work marked up: that's Gevurah, and it can be loving. Some teachers say even the making of the world needed both: love to give, and limits to give it shape. Neither side is meant to win. Too much of either, kabbalists say, and the world tips over.
screen: `TWO ARMS: ONE REACHES, ONE HOLDS.` · `ABRAHAM'S TENT, ISAAC'S AWE.` · `WATER AND FIRE.` · `LIMITS ARE A KIND OF CARE.` · then, large: `LOVE AND LIMITS.`

segments.voice: Let your right hand rest open on your knee and think of one place where you give, maybe until it floods; then let your left hand close gently and think of one place where you hold back, maybe until it burns. Rest both hands still, and ask, without judging yourself, which one needs a little more of the other.
Chesed. Love and kindness, giving freely: the right arm of the sefirot, linked to Abraham and to water, held in balance by Gevurah, strength and restraint. Today's word.
Your line: chesed gives freely; gevurah gives it shape. A river needs both water and banks. Tomorrow, the light in the middle.

1178.title: Tiferet, the heart of the tree
1178.hook: beauty that balances love and strength
1178.carry: tiferet holds love and strength in harmony
1178.howItsDone: In Kabbalah, Tiferet is taught as the central sefirah that harmonizes Chesed and Gevurah; Hasidic teaching applies it to a balanced heart, often through the figure of Jacob.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chesed and Gevurah: the river and its banks, Abraham's open tent and Isaac's awe. Your line: chesed gives freely; gevurah gives it shape. Today, the light that holds them together.
screen: `CHESED GIVES FREELY; GEVURAH GIVES IT SHAPE.`

segments.voice: A guitar string tuned too loose just flaps and buzzes. Tuned too tight, it snaps. Somewhere between, there's a point where it rings, and you can hear the moment it arrives. That point isn't half loose and half tight. It's something else entirely: a note. Love and limits pull in two directions, right arm and left arm. The kabbalists put a third light in the middle, and they didn't call it compromise, or average, or fairness. They called it beauty.
screen: `TOO LOOSE, IT BUZZES.` → `TOO TIGHT, IT SNAPS.` → `BETWEEN, IT RINGS.`

segments.voice: Tiferet. Beauty, glory, harmony. First, where it sits. On the kabbalists' map, Tiferet stands in the center, below Chesed and Gevurah, holding them together. Some teachers draw the whole tree in three columns: love on the right, strength on the left, and a middle column running straight down through Tiferet. Second, you've already heard it. Three days ago, in David's blessing: "the greatness, and the power, and the glory." That word glory, in Hebrew, is tiferet. It was in the list all along. Third, its face. Micah's verse gave "the mercy to Abraham"; it begins with "the truth to Jacob". Kabbalists link Jacob to Tiferet, and Tiferet to truth: the son of Isaac and the grandson of Abraham, holding both inheritances in one life. Truth, in this picture, isn't harsh and isn't soft. It's what you get when love and strength are both honest. Fourth, the surprise. Harmony here isn't the absence of tension. A chord has notes that differ. A face is beautiful partly because its features aren't all the same. Tiferet keeps Chesed and Gevurah fully alive and lets them sound together. That's why the kabbalists didn't call it the middle. They called it beauty. Some teachers also call Tiferet the heart of the map, where the lights meet before they flow on, down toward the world.
screen: `THE CENTER OF THE MAP.` · `GLORY, IN DAVID'S BLESSING.` · `JACOB, AND TRUTH.` · `NOT HALF AND HALF: A CHORD.` · then, large: `HARMONY.`

segments.voice: Let your breath be the string: breathe in a little too long and notice the strain, out a little too short and notice the rush, then let it find the length where it rings. Stay there a while, then bring to mind one part of your life that's too loose or too tight. Don't fix it; just ask what the note would sound like if both sides were honest.
Tiferet. Beauty and harmony: the center of the sefirot, holding love and strength together, linked to Jacob and to truth. Today's word.

1179.title: Endurance, splendor, foundation
1179.hook: Netzach, Hod, Yesod: the lower sefirot that carry action into the world
1179.howItsDone: In Kabbalah, Netzach, Hod and Yesod are taught as the sefirot that carry the higher qualities into action; Hasidic teaching applies them to perseverance, humility and keeping one's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tiferet: the string that rings between too loose and too tight, beauty at the center of the map. Your line: harmony. Today, the lights below the heart.

Somewhere in the house, there's a drawer with one in it. The half-knitted scarf. The guitar with one lesson behind it. The notebook with a few good pages and then nothing. The idea was real. The love for it was real. Even the balance was there, for a while. What ran out was something plainer: the part that keeps walking after the excitement wears off, and the part that sets the thing down in the world where someone can use it. Kabbalists gave those parts their own lights.
screen: `THE HALF-KNITTED SCARF.` → `THE IDEA WAS REAL.` → `WHAT RAN OUT WAS PLAINER.`

segments.voice: Netzach, Hod, Yesod. Endurance, splendor, foundation. First, the body. Kabbalists sometimes picture the sefirot as a human figure. Chesed and Gevurah are the arms. Tiferet is the torso, the heart. And Netzach and Hod are the two legs. Arms reach and hold. Legs walk, carrying what was felt above into motion. Second, the pair. Netzach, on the right, is endurance, victory, the push to keep going. Hod, on the left, is splendor, and some teachers hear in it acknowledgment, even thanks: knowing when to yield, to adjust, to say this part isn't working. Push only, and you march off a cliff. Yield only, and you never leave the room. Third, the faces. Some traditions link Netzach to Moses, who pressed on through the long years in the desert, and Hod to Aaron, who served in the sanctuary. Two brothers, two ways of carrying a people. Fourth, the foundation. Below them sits Yesod, where everything above gathers before it reaches the world. The book of Proverbs says "the righteous is an everlasting foundation," and kabbalists linked Yesod to the righteous person, and to Joseph, who kept faith in a strange land and fed the hungry. So the lower lights aren't lesser lights. They're the ones that get the scarf finished, the meal on the table, the promise kept.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small unfinished thing, a reply you owe, a drawer half sorted, a page half read, and picture yourself doing the last step, the plain, unglamorous one. Notice where you'd want to push on, and where you might adjust the plan so it can actually get done, and breathe into both.
Endurance. Netzach: the light of pressing on, paired with Hod, splendor, and resting on Yesod, the foundation that carries everything into the world. Today's word.
Your line: endure. The lower lights are the ones that finish things. See you tomorrow.

1180.title: The indwelling presence
1180.hook: the presence of God in the world, often pictured as feminine
1180.howItsDone: Jews speak of the Shechinah in prayer and study, and some families, following a custom of the kabbalists, sing to welcome the Sabbath as a bride and queen on Friday evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Netzach and Hod, the two legs that walk, resting on Yesod, the foundation. Your line: endure. Today, where all the lights land.

"And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." That's God speaking to Moses in the book of Exodus, in the desert, before a single tent pole has gone up. Some readers have stopped on the last words. Not in it, in the building. Among them, in the people. A tent of cloth and wood, carried from camp to camp, and the promise is that God will live in the middle of all that walking and arguing and cooking. The rabbis gave that nearness a name that echoes the verse's own word for dwell.
screen: `MAKE ME A SANCTUARY.` → `NOT IN IT. AMONG THEM.` → `GOD IN THE MIDDLE OF THE CAMP.`

segments.voice: Shechinah. The indwelling presence of God. First, the rabbis' word for God close at hand. Pirkei Avot teaches that when people sit together and their talk is words of Torah, the Shechinah rests among them. Not in a temple. At a table. Second, it goes where the people go. The Talmud says that wherever Israel was exiled, the Shechinah went into exile with them. The presence doesn't stay behind in a ruined building. It packs its bags. Third, Kabbalah. The last of the ten lights is Malchut, kingship, the one that touches the world, and kabbalists identify it with the Shechinah. Every light above flows down into her. And notice the her. Kabbalists picture the Shechinah as feminine: a queen, a bride, sometimes a mother. Some Jews welcome the Sabbath on Friday night with songs that greet a bride and a queen, and kabbalists heard the Shechinah in those images. Fourth, the longing. In kabbalistic teaching, the Shechinah is in some sense separated, in exile, and human deeds of Torah, prayer and kindness help reunite her with the Holy One above. A reader might hear it this way: every good act, a little homecoming. In this teaching, the God without end, from a few days ago, is also the presence at the table.
screen: `PRESENCE AT A TABLE.` · `SHE GOES INTO EXILE TOO.` · `MALCHUT: WHERE THE LIGHTS LAND.` · `GOOD DEEDS AS HOMECOMING.` · then, large: `PRESENCE DWELLS.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes move slowly around the space you're in, the light on the wall, the chair, the sounds from outside, and any people near, without looking at them too hard. Shechinah. The indwelling presence of God, among the people and with them in exile; in Kabbalah, Malchut, pictured as a queen and a bride. Today's word.
Your line: presence dwells. Not only in a building, but at a table. Same time tomorrow.

1181.title: The Zohar's companions on the road
1181.hook: the Zohar's sages walk the roads of Galilee, teaching as they go
1181.carry: where companions talk torah, the presence walks along
1181.howItsDone: The Zohar is often studied in pairs or small circles, reading aloud together, and some study groups take walks or journeys to sites in Galilee linked to its sages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shechinah: the presence that dwells among the people, at a table, and even in exile. Your line: presence dwells. Today, the presence on the road.

Two rabbis are walking on a road. Dust, heat, hills, a long way still to go. One says to the other: let's open our mouths with words of Torah, so the walk isn't wasted. An old man trudges along with them, driving a donkey, a hired hand as far as they can tell. Then the donkey driver starts to talk, and out of his mouth come teachings that leave the two rabbis astonished. The Zohar, a central book of Kabbalah, tells scenes like this. Here, the teaching happens on the road.
screen: `TWO RABBIS ON A ROAD.` → `A DONKEY DRIVER BEHIND THEM.` → `TEACHING THAT HAPPENS WALKING.`

segments.voice: Companions on the road. In Aramaic, the Zohar calls them the chevraya, the companions. First, who they are. Tradition ties the Zohar to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a sage of the Mishnah, and the book tells of him and his circle walking the roads of the land of Israel, Galilee and beyond, teaching as they go. Scholars ask hard questions about when the book was written, and there are different answers. Either way, inside the book, this is the scene: friends, walking, talking Torah. Second, why the road. Yesterday: when people sit together and their talk is Torah, the Shechinah rests among them. The Zohar's companions carry that onto the road; its sages say that when travelers speak words of Torah, the presence joins them on the way. A road becomes a moving sanctuary. Third, the stranger. More than once in the Zohar, the teacher turns out to be someone the companions overlooked: an old donkey driver, a child, a traveler on the road. Wisdom may be walking just behind them. Fourth, companionship itself. In these stories, nobody learns alone. One companion asks a question, another answers, a third sees something new in the answer, and Rabbi Shimon praises them when they get it right. The secrets of the Torah, in this picture, open up between people, in conversation, on the way somewhere.
screen: `THE CHEVRAYA, THE COMPANIONS.` · `TORAH ON THE ROAD.` · `THE STRANGER WHO TEACHES.` · `NOBODY LEARNS ALONE.` · then, large: `COMPANIONS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you'd like to walk beside, a friend, a sibling, someone you've lost touch with, and picture the road and the ground under your feet. Then hold one real question you'd want to ask them, not small talk, something about what matters to them, and keep the question and their face together for a while.
Companions on the road. The chevraya of the Zohar: friends walking together, teaching Torah as they go, and finding wisdom in strangers. Today's words.
Your line: where companions talk torah, the presence walks along. The book itself teaches like a walk with friends. Rest well.

1182.title: The Torah's garments (Zohar 3:152a)
1182.hook: the stories are the Torah's clothing; look for the soul inside
1182.howItsDone: This Zohar passage is taught in Jewish study as a way of reading Torah on more than one level, and the plain sense of the story is still learned first, with deeper readings built on top of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sages of the Zohar walked the roads of Galilee, teaching as they went. Your line: companions on the road. Today, how they read the Torah itself.

A person walks down the street in a beautiful coat. Many passersby see only the coat. A few notice the person wearing it: how they walk, the look on their face. Fewer still wonder what that person is like inside, what they love, what keeps them up at night. The Zohar takes that ordinary street and turns it into a way of reading. Its sages say the Torah walks among us dressed, too. And they ask a sharp question about what we've been looking at all along.
screen: `A COAT ON THE STREET.` → `THE PERSON INSIDE IT.` → `THE TORAH, DRESSED.`

segments.voice: The Torah's garments. The passage sits in the Zohar's section on the book of Numbers, and it opens with something close to a dare. If the Torah were only stories about ordinary people, it says, we could write a book like that ourselves, perhaps even a finer one. So the stories must be more than they look. First, the garment. The Zohar says the tales of the Torah are its clothing. Abraham bargaining, Jacob wrestling, a donkey that speaks. They're real and worth reading, and they're also what the Torah is wearing. Second, the body. Under the garment, the Zohar says, is the body of the Torah, and it names the commandments as that body: the shape the Torah takes in a life. Third, the soul. Inside the body is the soul, the innermost Torah, and the passage says the wise, the ones who stood at Sinai, look only there. Fourth, the people looking. The Zohar sorts readers like passersby on the street. Some see only the clothing, and stop. Some see the body under it. And some look through both to the soul. Notice what the passage doesn't do. It doesn't throw the garment away. Clothing is how a body moves among people; without it, nobody would meet the Torah at all. The Zohar's complaint is only with the reader who thinks the coat is the whole person. So the stories stay. They're the doorway, not the whole house.
screen: `STORIES ARE ITS CLOTHING.` · `THE COMMANDMENTS ARE ITS BODY.` · `INSIDE, THE SOUL.` · `THREE KINDS OF READERS.` · then, large: `LOOK BENEATH THE GARMENT.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing near you, a cup, a coat on a hook, a photo, and look at its surface: its color, its shape, how it sits. Then go one layer down, who made it and what it's for, and if you like, one more: what it carries for you or someone you love. No need to find anything grand; just keep going under, gently, one layer at a time.

Your line: look beneath the garment. A coat is never the whole person. I'll be here tomorrow.

1183.title: Contraction
1183.hook: Luria taught that God withdrew to make room for a world
1183.howItsDone: Tzimtzum is studied in Lurianic Kabbalah through Chaim Vital's Etz Chaim and its commentaries, and Hasidic teachers return to it often, especially in discussions of how God can be everywhere and a world can still exist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zohar dressed the Torah in stories, with a body and a soul underneath. Your line: look beneath the garment. Today, a teacher in Safed asks where a world could fit.

Before anyone new can sit at a crowded table, somebody has to scoot over. A small thing. A chair pulled back, a bag moved, an elbow tucked in. The table doesn't grow. The people already at it draw in a little. In the town of Safed, a teacher named Isaac Luria, whom his students called the Ari, asked something like it about everything there is. If God is without end and fills all things, where was there room for a world? His answer begins with a drawing in.
screen: `SOMEBODY HAS TO SCOOT OVER.` → `GOD FILLS ALL THINGS.` → `WHERE IS THERE ROOM?`

segments.voice: Tzimtzum. The Hebrew means a contraction, a narrowing, a drawing in. Luria's teaching reaches us through his student Chaim Vital, in a work called Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life. First, the problem. Before anything was made, Vital writes, the light of the Infinite, the Ein Sof we met not long ago, filled everything. There was no empty space at all. Nowhere for a world to be. Second, the withdrawing. So the Infinite drew itself in, away from a center, and left an open space: a place where something other than God could exist. In this picture, creation starts with a stepping back. Third, the thin line. Into that open space, Vital writes, came a single line of light, reaching in from the Infinite. The space is never cut off. Whatever lives there is held by that thread. Fourth, the argument. Later teachers disagreed about how to read this. Some took the withdrawal at its word. Others, Hasidic teachers among them, said God never truly leaves any place, and the contraction is a hiding, so the world can have a place of its own. Both readings keep a God who makes space rather than taking it all. And some readers hear a human echo in it. A parent who goes quiet so a child can try. A teacher who leaves a question open. A friend who lets you finish your own sentence.
screen: `NO ROOM FOR A WORLD.` · `THE INFINITE DRAWS IN.` · `A SINGLE LINE OF LIGHT.` · `READ AS LEAVING, OR AS HIDING.` · then, large: `MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who could use a little more space from you: maybe you talk over them, fix things before they've asked, or fill every silence. Picture the next time you're together, and see yourself leaving a pause, not walking away, just drawing in a little so there's room. Rest there, and notice what might grow in that space: their words, their idea, their own way of doing it.
Tzimtzum. Contraction: in Luria's teaching, the Infinite drawing in to leave room for a world. Today's word.
Your line: make room. Creation, in this picture, starts with a stepping back. See you tomorrow.
